description: I'm a STEM high school student passionate about space technology, AI, software development, and solving real-world problems through innovation. I'm currently building a team for LUNARITHM, a project idea for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge.
summary:
LUNARITHM is a web tool that helps mission planners choose where and when to land on the Moon. Most site-selection tools just give you a ranked list. We wanted to answer the harder questions: which site fits this mission best, what are we giving up by picking it, and how much would our priorities have to change before a different site wins?
We built it around real Sun and Earth positions, calculated with the astronomy-engine library, including libration and the changing Earth–Moon distance. You can pick a south-pole site, scrub through any date, and see in 3D and on a sky plot when the Sun and Earth are above the horizon. That matters for power and for talking to Earth. On top of that we added a decision engine that ranks sites two different ways, shows the exact point where the top choice flips, and tests the result across 300 scenarios. A physics lab covers battery, radio link, and temperature estimates.
Site choice is never one-size-fits-all, so we made the reasoning visible. Every number is labeled by where it came from (measured, derived, estimated), and users can import real LRO LOLA terrain data to replace our placeholder horizons.
details:
LUNARITHM runs entirely in the browser. You choose a candidate landing site, set your mission priorities and hard limits (such as minimum sunlight or Earth visibility), and pick a date range. The app then works out where the Sun and Earth sit in the lunar sky for every hour of that period. It uses the astronomy-engine library for the positions, and accounts for libration, the changing Earth–Moon distance, and the way an airless horizon dips below flat. The results show up in a 3D terrain view, a sky-dome plot, and a timeline you can scrub through.

From there, the decision tools take over. Sites are ranked with two different methods (weighted sum and TOPSIS) so you can see whether they agree. A flip detector calculates the exact weight change needed for a different site to take first place, and a weight-space map shows where each site wins. We also run 300 randomized priority scenarios to check whether the top pick holds up, and a minimax regret view shows the safest choice if you’re unsure what matters most. Other panels cover landing dispersion, a five-role stakeholder room, and a value-of-information view that points to which missing data would change the answer most. A physics lab estimates battery charge, the Earth radio link, surface temperature, and whether two outposts can reach each other.

The benefit is that planners can see why a site wins and how fragile that win is, instead of trusting a single score. We hope it helps teams argue about trade-offs with evidence, and helps students and the public see how lunar site selection works.

For tools, we used React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, Three.js for the 3D views, and astronomy-engine for ephemeris. We built it with Google AI Studio. All the science lives in separate, testable TypeScript modules, with a 14-test self-test that passes.

The default horizon profiles are synthetic placeholders, and users can replace them by importing real LRO LOLA data. Results can be shared through links and exported as JSON, CSV, or a written rationale memo.
